content: The navel, also known as the belly button or umbilicus, is a scar located on the abdomen. This scar forms as a result of the removal of the umbilical cord from a newborn baby. All placental mammals possess a navel, though its appearance varies significantly between species. In humans, the navel is relatively prominent, whereas in most other mammals, it is typically a thin, hairless line. In humans, the navel can present as either a depression (commonly referred to as an innie) or a protrusion (known as an outie). However, navels exhibit considerable variation in size, shape, depth, and overall appearance among individuals. Since the navel is essentially a scar and not determined by genetics, it can serve as a distinguishing feature between identical twins in the absence of other identifiable marks. The navel is an important anatomical landmark on the human abdomen due to its relatively consistent position across individuals. The skin around the waist at the level of the navel is innervated by the tenth thoracic spinal nerve (T10 dermatome). The navel itself is located at the level between the L3 and L4 vertebrae. Approximately 90% of people have an innie, while the remaining 10% have an outie. The formation of an outie is often due to excess skin left from the umbilical cord or the presence of an umbilical hernia, though not all children with umbilical hernias develop an outie. Beneath the visible depression of the navel, the underlying abdominal muscle layers also exhibit a concavity. This structural thinness contributes to a relative weakness in this area, making it more susceptible to hernias. During pregnancy, the expanding uterus exerts pressure on the navel, often causing it to protrude outward. After childbirth, the navel typically retracts to its original position. The navel is also used as a reference point to visually divide the abdomen into quadrants. In Leonardo da Vinci's famous drawing, the Vitruvian Man, the navel is depicted as the central point of the circle that encloses the spread-eagle figure. This illustrates the principle that, while the apparent center of the body may shift between different poses, the navel, as the true center of gravity, remains stationary. The height of the navel on the abdomen varies among individuals. An ideal navel height, relative to body height, is often associated with the Golden Section or Divine Proportion, a geometric ratio celebrated by philosophers and artists. This ideal proportion places the navel at approximately 62% of the total body height, creating a visually harmonious balance between the legs and torso. Cultural attitudes toward the navel have varied widely. In certain Western cultures, displaying a bare navel has historically been considered taboo due to its perceived erotic undertones, particularly in the case of innies. For example, in the 1960s, actress Barbara Eden was prohibited from showing her navel on the television show I Dream of Jeannie. However, the modern trend of exposing the navel, particularly among women, has become more accepted in Western societies. This trend includes the popularity of navel piercings and tattoos, often showcased with short shirts or low-rise clothing. In contrast, Indian culture has long embraced the display of the navel, particularly through traditional attire such as saris, which intentionally expose the midriff. In this context, the navel is not considered taboo but is instead regarded as a graceful and symbolic feature, often associated with femininity, fertility, and life. A dimpled navel is even considered a desirable trait for prospective brides, especially in South India, and is celebrated in Bollywood cinema. Among certain Indian communities, such as the Rajasthanis and Gujaratis, women traditionally wear short blouses (cholis) with skirts that expose the midriff, while simultaneously covering their heads and faces in the presence of strangers. This duality underscores the navel's symbolic association with birth, life, and the nurturing role of nature. The navel has also been a subject of sexual fascination and fetishism, particularly among males. While the cleavage of breasts is often overtly associated with feminine allure, the navel is seen as a subtler emblem of femininity, combining innocence with sexual appeal. In the Song of Solomon from the Old Testament, the navel is poetically praised alongside other parts of the female body, such as the belly and thighs, as a symbol of beauty and sensuality. Modern interpretations, such as those by Deirdre Day-MacLeod, suggest that the navel's allure lies in its lack of obvious purpose, combined with its bold and central placement on the body, which draws attention and admiration. In mythology, the navel has also been linked to beauty and love. For instance, the Italian pasta tortellini is said to represent the navel of Venus, the Roman goddess of love (known as Aphrodite in Greek mythology).
